title: OpenAI expands its Stargate community pact: no NDAs with officials, full power costs covered
subtitle: The new policy blueprint hardens earlier promises into written commitments as communities near proposed Stargate sites push back on utility-cost and water-use concerns.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: OpenAI this week published an expanded policy blueprint for its Stargate data-center build-out, committing to two concrete things that go beyond its January 2026 Stargate Community plan. First, it pledges to use no non-disclosure agreements with elected or appointed public officials when siting a facility. Second, it promises to cover the full cost of incremental electricity and grid infrastructure at facilities it owns — not just a share, and not just at off-grid sites.

The specifics matter because the January plan was criticized for leaving wiggle room. 'Pay our way on energy' can mean many things when a hyperscale load drops into a regulated-utility rate base. The new commitment to pay the full incremental cost — and the ban on NDAs with public officials — closes two of the loopholes that local-government critics and clean-energy groups had flagged. Microsoft rolled out a similar utility-rate pledge earlier this year, and the two companies' plans are now roughly aligned.

The context is a build-out at an unprecedented scale. Stargate's announced site footprint runs into the hundreds of billions of dollars and gigawatts of load, and residents near proposed sites in Texas, Ohio, and New Mexico have already filed objections over water, tax breaks, and electricity-rate impacts. Voluntary pacts of this kind do not have the force of law, but they do set expectations against which future complaints will be measured.

A takeaway for learners: 'self-regulation' in AI infrastructure almost always starts as a voluntary pledge in response to specific community pressure, then gets codified when a utility commission or a state legislature decides to write it into law. If you are trying to anticipate where AI regulation will land next, read the local hearings in data-center counties — that is where the next generation of binding rules is being drafted in plain language.
